newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: New steps seen having muted impact on S'pore shares.
newsitem.headline: New steps seen having muted impact on S'pore shares.

text.p: New government steps to boost Singapore capital markets are expected to reap benefits in the long run but in the short term do little to boost the sagging local bourse, market analysts and brokers said on Wednesday.
They said the move to allow foreign firms to denominate shares in Singapore dollars was among the more significant of the measures announced on Tuesday by Finance Minister Richard Hu.
It could potentially increase liquidity and retail interest in such stock, analysts said.

"Hopefully, in the longer term it would encourage more foreign firms to have primary listings here and eventually that might create more volume and benefit the banking industry," said Ang Lay Pheng, vice president of Asia investment research with Goldman Sachs.
Finance Minister Hu said the move was in line with Monetary Authority of Singapore policy to allow gradual internationalisation of the Singapore dollar.

But brokers noted several conditions were attached to qualifying for a Singapore dollar listing, including a clause requiring companies to have 35 percent of revenue, profit or expense attributed to their Singapore operations.
"Most of the foreign companies already listed here do not qualify. Definitely, not the Jardine group of companies," said the director of a local broking firm.
Of the 40-odd foreign companies already listed in Singapore, brokers said less than a handful would qualify to convert their foreign currency denominated shares to Singapore dollars.
Shipping-based Osprey Maritime Ltd and systems integrator Datacraft Asia Ltd are said to be among the few that might qualify.

"We are investigating to see if we can qualify. We are interested. We have to see if we can comply with the conditions that will allow us to trade in Singapore dollar," Erling Strom, managing director of Osprey, told Reuters.
Datacraft chief operating officer Des Althorp also said his company would be checking to see if it could qualify to convert.

He told Reuters that Datacraft, which has a wide following with institutional investors, would also be asking for feedback from fund managers and its board of directors to see if the company should make the switch.

"It is a step in the right direction. But the exchange needs to fully liberalise Singapore dollar listings in order to attract more foreign firms," said one broker who added that the 35 percent requirement was seen as a hurdle.

Dealers said other measures announced by Hu, like the launch of a regional index and a S$50 million (US$35 million) fund to invest in the index shares, would do little for the local stock market, sold down in recent months on the back of a slowing economy.
The key Straits Times Industrial index is down some 17 percent from its year high of 2,493 in early February.
On Wednesday, the Straits Times Industrial Index closed up 10.78 points to 2,071.26, off an intraday high of 2,079.26.
Hu's announcement of a shortened settlement period of three days from the current five days for share transactions by 1997 had a mixed impact on the market.

"The shorter settlement period would hit contra traders but would benefit fund managers in the long term as they can get their money quicker," said an institutional dealer with a local broking firm. (US$1 = S$1.41)
